\chapter{Days of the Week}
\label{ch:hi-days-of-the-week}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name all seven days of the week in Hindi and say which planet each day is named for.}

Recite \hi{सोमवार} through \hi{रविवार} end to end, naming Saturn's day and the Sun's day to close the planet-week.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{सोमवार} \hi{मंगलवार} \hi{बुधवार} \hi{गुरुवार} \hi{शुक्रवार}]{\hi{सोमवार} to \hi{शुक्रवार} — Hindi's own planet-week}

\label{lesson:HI-C10-somavaar-shukravaar}



\begin{quote}
You've seen Spanish, Latin, and French name their weekdays for planet-gods. Here's the surprise: \textbf{Hindi does too} — with its own, independent set of gods.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The pattern: {[}deity{]} + \hi{वार}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}}
Every Hindi weekday is a \textbf{deity's name} plus \textbf{\hi{वार}} (\emph{vār}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} (Sanskrit \emph{vāra}):

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{literally} & \textbf{deity/planet} & \textbf{day} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\hi{सोमवार}} (\emph{somavār}) & Soma's day & the \textbf{Moon} & Monday \\
\textbf{\hi{मंगलवार}} (\emph{maṅgalvār}) & Mangala's day & \textbf{Mars} & Tuesday \\
\textbf{\hi{बुधवार}} (\emph{budhvār}) & Budha's day & \textbf{Mercury} & Wednesday \\
\textbf{\hi{गुरुवार}} (\emph{guruvār}) & Guru's day & \textbf{Jupiter} (\emph{Bṛhaspati}, called \textquotedblleft{}Guru,\textquotedblright{} teacher of the gods) & Thursday \\
\textbf{\hi{शुक्रवार}} (\emph{śukravār}) & Śukra's day & \textbf{Venus} & Friday \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about where this system came from}
This is \textbf{the same seven-body idea} as Rome's planetary week — Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn — and it is \textbf{not} an isolated Indian invention: historians trace it, ultimately, to a shared source in \textbf{Babylonian astronomy}, and most accounts hold that it reached both Rome and India through the \textbf{same Hellenistic-Greek channel} of transmission (India's own horoscopic-astrology texts, like the \emph{Yavanajātaka}, are explicitly adapted from Greek originals). The exact path and timing into India are still debated among historians of astronomy, but the system isn't a case of Rome and India copying each other directly — both are more like \textbf{cousins}, downstream of one much older shared idea of the sky.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}somavār\textquotedblright{} — Soma/Moon's day — then \textquotedblleft{}maṅgalvār,\textquotedblright{} Mangala/Mars's day
  \item the pattern — \textquotedblleft{}{[}deity{]} + vār\textquotedblright{} = {[}deity{]}'s day
  \item \textquotedblleft{}guruvār\textquotedblright{} — Thursday — Bṛhaspati, called \textquotedblleft{}Guru\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does every Hindi weekday end in, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\hi{वार}} \emph{vār}, \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}) Which planet is \textbf{\hi{गुरुवार}}, and what title does its deity carry? (\textbf{Jupiter} — the deity Bṛhaspati, called \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Guru},\textquotedblright{} teacher of the gods — an ancient title Bṛhaspati bears, not the source of the word itself.) Did Hindi borrow its planet-week from Rome? (\textbf{No} — both likely trace back through \textbf{Hellenistic Greece} to a shared \textbf{Babylonian} astronomical source, though the exact route into India is still debated.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{शनिवार} \hi{रविवार}]{\hi{शनिवार} and \hi{रविवार} — Saturday and Sunday, no rewrite needed}

\label{lesson:HI-C10-shanivaar-ravivaar}



\begin{quote}
You've met five Hindi weekdays, each a deity's name plus \textbf{\hi{वार}} (\emph{vār}), \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{} The last two complete the set — and here, unlike Spanish or French, \textbf{nothing ever got renamed}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The last two days}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{शनिवार}} (\emph{śanivār}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Śani's day}\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{Saturn}.
  \item \textbf{\hi{रविवार}} (\emph{ravivār}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Ravi's day}\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{Sun} (\emph{Ravi}, one of the Sun's many Sanskrit names).
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about the contrast with Spanish and French}
Remember: Spanish's \textbf{sábado}/\textbf{domingo} and French's \textbf{samedi}/\textbf{dimanche} are \textbf{not} simple planet-names — Christianity renamed both (Saturn's day became the \emph{Sabbath}; the Sun's day became \textquotedblleft{}\emph{the Lord's day}\textquotedblright{}). Hindi's weekend went through \textbf{no such rewrite}: \textbf{\hi{शनिवार}} and \textbf{\hi{रविवार}} are still, today, plainly \textquotedblleft{}Saturn's day\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Sun's day\textquotedblright{} — the full planet-week, all seven days, standing untouched by any later religious relabeling.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śanivār\textquotedblright{} — Saturn's day — then \textquotedblleft{}ravivār,\textquotedblright{} Sun's day
  \item the whole week — \textquotedblleft{}somavār, maṅgalvār, budhvār, guruvār, śukravār, śanivār, ravivār\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — Spanish/French renamed their weekend; Hindi never did
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \textbf{\hi{शनिवार}} and \textbf{\hi{रविवार}} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Saturn's day\textquotedblright{}} and \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Sun's day.\textquotedblright{}}) How is Hindi's weekend different from Spanish's or French's? (\textbf{No religious rewrite ever happened} — Hindi kept the plain planet-names for all seven days, while Spanish/French swapped in \emph{Sabbath} / \emph{Lord's day} for the weekend.)
\end{tcolorbox}
